Dudeney’s Dissection is Optimal

Erik D. Demaine    Tonan Kamata    Ryuhei Uehara
Abstract

In 1907, Henry Ernest Dudeney posed a puzzle: “cut any equilateral triangle … into as few pieces as possible that will fit together and form a perfect square” (without overlap, via translation and rotation). Four weeks later, Dudeney demonstrated a beautiful four-piece solution, which today remains perhaps the most famous example of dissection. In this paper (over a century later), we finally solve Dudeney’s puzzle, by proving that the equilateral triangle and square have no common dissection with three or fewer polygonal pieces. We reduce the problem to the analysis of discrete graph structures representing the correspondence between the edges and the vertices of the pieces forming each polygon.

1 Introduction

Dissection [15, 9] is the process of transforming one shape AA into another shape BB by cutting AA into pieces and re-arranging those pieces to form BB (without overlap). Necessarily, AA and BB must have the same area (a property Euclid used to prove area equalities). Conversely, every two polygons of the same area have a dissection — a result from over two centuries ago [16, 18, 2, 13]. The number of pieces cannot be bounded as a function of the number of vertices (consider, for example, dissecting an N×NN\times N square into an N2×1N^{2}\times 1 rectangle), but there is a pseudopolynomial upper bound [1].

Given two specific polygons, can we find the dissection between them with the fewest possible pieces? In general, this minimization problem is NP-hard, even to approximate within a factor of 1+1/1080−ε1+1/1080-\varepsilon [3]. Worse, the existence of a kk-piece dissection is not known to be decidable, even for k=2k=2 pieces [3]. A core difficulty is that the number of cut segments has no obvious upper bound, even for 2-piece dissection. The special case where the k=2k=2 pieces must be mirror congruent to each other has a polynomial-time decision algorithm [8], even though the number of cuts cannot be bounded as a function of nn [17].

Instances of the dissection problem have captivated puzzle creators and solvers for centuries; see [9, 12] for much history. One pioneer was English puzzlist Henry Ernest Dudeney [11], who published many dissection puzzles in newspapers and magazines in the late 19th and early 20th centuries [6, 7]. Over the years, geometric puzzlers continually improved the records for the fewest-piece dissections between various pairs of polygons. Harry Lindgren (an Australian patent reviewer) collected many of these results and improved most of them in his book [15]. He wrote:

“In a few cases (very, very few) it could perhaps be rigorously proved that the minimum number has been attained, and in a few more one can feel morally certain; in all the rest it is possible that you may find a dissection that is better than those already known” [15, p. 1]

Some past work determines the asymptotic growth of the number of pieces for certain infinite families. Cohn [4] showed that a triangle of diameter dd needs Θ⁡(d)\Theta(d) pieces to dissect into a unit square, where the constant in the Θ\Theta is between 0.74150.7415 and 11. (The obvious diameter lower bound is d/2≈0.7071​dd/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.7071\,d.) Kranakis, Krizanc, and Urrutia [14] showed that the regular nn-gon needs Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) pieces to dissect into a square, where the constant in the Θ\Theta is between 1/41/4 and 1/21/2.

In this paper, we give the first nontrivial proof of exact optimality of the number of pieces in a dissection, by proving optimality of the famous four-piece dissection of an equilateral triangle to a square shown in Figure 1. Dudeney [5] posed this dissection as a puzzle on April 6, 1902, without making it especially clear whether he had a solution. In the next issue of his column (April 20), he described an easy five-piece solution, wrote that Mr. C. W. McElroy of Manchester had found a four-piece solution, and gave readers another two weeks to try to find it. No one did, leading Dudeney to conclude that “the puzzle may be regarded as a decidedly hard nut” in the next issue where he gave the four-piece solution (May 4). It remains unclear whether this solution was originally invented by Dudeney or McElroy [9, 10]. The puzzle and solution appeared later in Dudeney’s book as “The Haberdasher’s Puzzle” [6, Puzzle 26]; Gardner [11] called it “Dudeney’s best-known geometrical discovery”.

Since this discovery over 120 years ago, it has remained open whether this dissection is optimal, or whether the record will someday be improved upon (as many other records have) [5, 1, 3]. In this paper, we finally settle this problem:

Theorem 1.

There is no dissection with three or fewer polygonal pieces between a square and an equilateral triangle, when we forbid flipping pieces.

Figure 1 also does not require the pieces to be flipped, but this is not necessarily a requirement in the original puzzle. When first teasing “the correct solution”, Dudeney wrote, “surprising as it may seem, it is not necessary to turn over any piece.” So we leave an intriguing puzzle for future work: is there a 3-piece dissection if we allow flipping pieces? We also do not know whether curved pieces might help, though we suspect Theorem 1 extends to both of these settings.

1.1 Overview

The structure of the proof is as follows. First, it is relatively easy to show that a two-piece dissection is impossible (see Lemma 14). Thus, we focus on proving the impossibility of a three-piece dissection. To do so, we classify the finitely many possible topologies for cutting each polygon that could potentially result in a three-piece dissection. Next, we use fundamental properties of dissections to narrow down the feasible combinations of these cutting topologies for the two shapes. Finally, we show that all remaining combinations are infeasible using the new concepts of “matching diagrams”, which handle the potentially unbounded number of cut segments.

This paper is organized as follows. We start in Section 2 with basic definitions of dissections, specifically the graph of cuts within each shape, and a categorization of vertices in these graphs into six types. Then, in Section 3, we introduce our primary tool for analyzing dissections — vertex and edge matching diagrams — and prove several general necessary properties for dissections to work, which can be applied to other dissection problems as well. Next, in Section 4, we give a technical overview of our proof, and illustrate by describing one key case in detail; this section gives a flavor of our techniques without getting bogged down in the many cases necessary to complete the proof (but from a technical perspective, it can be skipped). Finally, in Section 5, we give the full proof, which applies the matching diagrams from Section 3 to the specific case of the equilateral triangle and the square.

2 Preliminaries

We define a polygon to be a connected region in the plane of finite area bounded by finitely many line segments. (This definition does not require polygons to be simple, although we will show in Lemma 16 that our main proof can consider just simple polygons.) We refer to a polygon’s line segments as sides and the intersections of these sides as corners.11 1 We use these terms (instead of more common terms such as “edges” and “vertices”) to provide unambiguous terminology for edge- and node-like features of various parallel structures: polygons, cut graphs, and matching graphs. The boundary of a polygon consists of the corners and points along the sides, while the interior is all other points within the region. Let |s||s| denote the Euclidean length of a side ss, and let ∠⁡(x)\angle(x) denote the interior angle of the region at corner xx.

A 𝒌k-piece dissection of a pair of polygons (P,P′)(P,P^{\prime}) consists of kk polygons P1,P2,…,PkP_{1},P_{2},\ldots,P_{k} and two sets of corresponding congruence transformations λ1,λ2,…,λk{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}} and λ1′,λ2′,…,λk′{\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\lambda^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,\lambda^{\prime}_{k}} such that ⨆iλi​(Pi)=P\bigsqcup_{i}\lambda_{i}(P_{i})=P and ⨆iλi′​(Pi)=P′\bigsqcup_{i}\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(P_{i})=P^{\prime}.22 2 The notation ⊔\sqcup denotes interior-disjoint set union, i.e., we allow the polygons to overlap on shared boundaries. Figure 1 is an example of a 4-piece dissection. We refer to PP and P′P^{\prime} as target shapes, and P1,P2,…,PkP_{1},P_{2},\ldots,P_{k} as pieces. Naturally, the areas of the target shapes must be equal to the total area of the pieces.

A dissection of (P,P′)(P,P^{\prime}) divides each target shape X∈{P,P′}X\in\{P,P^{\prime}\} into pieces by cut lines. We define a finite geometric graph called the cut graph GXG^{X}, which represents the cut lines and the boundary of XX. Specifically, GXG^{X} has faces that correspond one-to-one with the pieces, vertices V⁡(GX)V(G^{X}) which consist of the corners of XX and the points along the cut lines having at least one surrounding angle not equal to π\pi, and edges E⁡(GX)E(G^{X}) which consist of the cut and boundary lines connecting these vertices. For example, Figure 1 highlights the vertices and edges of GPG^{P} and GP′G^{P^{\prime}} for Dudeney’s four-piece dissection. The edges E⁡(GX)E(G^{X}) either originate from cut lines, referred to as internal edges, or from the sides of XX, referred to as boundary edges. The vertices V⁡(GX)V(G^{X}) are intersections between at least two edges; a vertex met only by internal edges is an internal vertex, while a vertex met by at least one boundary edge is a boundary vertex. Based on the elements surrounding each vertex of GXG^{X}, we classify boundary vertices into Types 1–2 and internal vertices into Types 3–6 as follows (refer to Figure 2):

  • •

    Type 1: Corner vertex. A boundary vertex corresponding to a corner of the target shape XX.

  • •

    Type 2: Side vertex. A boundary vertex corresponding to a point along a side of the target shape XX.

  • •

    Type 3: Paired vertex. An internal vertex where exactly two piece corners meet.

  • •

    Type 4: Convex vertex. An internal vertex where three or more piece corners meet, and all interior angles are convex.

  • •

    Type 5: Reflex vertex. An internal vertex where three or more piece corners meet and only one of them is reflex.

  • •

    Type 6: Flat vertex. An internal vertex where at least two piece corners and one piece side meet.

This distinction will be useful in Section 5.1 when counting the number of angles appearing in the cut graph.

We define a subdivision of the cut graph GXG^{X} to be a graph obtained by replacing internal edges of GXG^{X} with paths consisting of paired (Type 3) vertices. We define an equivalence relation ∼\sim where G0X∼G1XG^{X}_{0}\sim G^{X}_{1} if there exist subdivisions H0XH^{X}_{0} and H1XH^{X}_{1} of the graphs G0XG^{X}_{0} and G1XG^{X}_{1} respectively, and a bijection ϕ:V⁡(H0X)→V⁡(H1X)\phi:V(H^{X}_{0})\rightarrow V(H^{X}_{1}) such that ϕ\phi is a graph isomorphism that disregards geometry while preserving vertex types.

3 Matching Diagram

When a set of pieces is assembled to form a target shape, each side of a piece corresponds to an edge of the cut graph, and each corner corresponds to a vertex of the cut graph. Therefore, when a pair of target shapes has a dissection, there are two corresponding relationships: one between the edges and another between the vertices of the cut graph. In this section, we formalize these relationships and describe these properties.

3.1 Edge Matching Diagram

When analyzing the relationship between the sides of pieces and the edges of the cut graph, the fundamental principle is that boundary edges correspond to a single side of a piece, while interior edges correspond to two sides from different pieces. However, this correspondence becomes more complex in the vicinity of flat vertices. For instance, when there is a flat vertex on the side of a piece, two sides of the pieces correspond to this side (see the left of Figure 3). Moreover, when multiple flat vertices are adjacent on the graph, more complex correspondences arise (see the middle and right of Figure 3).

To systematically represent these relationships, we introduce a bipartite diagram. In this diagram, each side of a piece is treated as a link, and the edges of the cut graph are treated as nodes. The endpoints of each link are the nodes representing the edges, which correspond to the sides indicated by the links. This construction ensures that an edge corresponding one-to-one to two sides becomes a degree-2 node, while all other edges become degree-1 nodes. In cases where a side crosses multiple edges due to flat vertices, we introduce virtual nodes (see the red lines in the left and the middle of Figure 3). In contrast, edges of the cut graph that do not correspond to any piece side are removed from the node set (see the red dotted line in the right of Figure 3). We now formalize this construction as follows:

Definition 2.

We define an edge matching diagram ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} for a pair of cut graphs GPG^{P} and GP′G^{P^{\prime}} (see Figure 4) as follows:

  • •

    For each X∈{P,P′}X\in\{P,P^{\prime}\}, define the node set NX​(ℰ​𝒟)N^{X}(\mathscr{ED}) as follows:

    • –

      Initialize NX​(ℰ​𝒟)N^{X}(\mathscr{ED}) as E⁡(GX)E(G^{X}).

    • –

      For an edge x∈NX​(ℰ​𝒟)x\in N^{X}(\mathscr{ED}), if both endpoints of xx in the cut graph are flat vertices and an angle of π\pi appears on opposite sides of xx, then remove xx from NX​(ℰ​𝒟)N^{X}(\mathscr{ED}).

    • –

      For each side of a piece xx, if there is a flat vertex on xx when forming XX, add a new corresponding node to NX​(ℰ​𝒟)N^{X}(\mathscr{ED}).

  • •

    Let L⁡(ℰ​𝒟)L(\mathscr{ED}) be the set of links between NP​(ℰ​𝒟)N^{P}(\mathscr{ED}) and NP′​(ℰ​𝒟)N^{P^{\prime}}(\mathscr{ED}), connecting a link for each side e∈E⁡(P1)∪E⁡(P2)∪⋯∪E⁡(Pk)e\in E(P_{1})\cup E(P_{2})\cup\cdots\cup E(P_{k}) according to the correspondence between links representing the sides of pieces and nodes representing the edges of the graph.

The added nodes corresponding to a flat vertex are called flat nodes, nodes corresponding to boundary edges are called boundary nodes, and all other nodes are called internal nodes. We use terms such as degree, leaf, and path for the diagram in the same way as they are used in standard graph theory.

By construction, the degree of each node in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} is either 11 or 22. Moreover, since two sides sharing a degree-2 node correspond to the same edge of a cut graph, their lengths are equal. Consequently, a path can be obtained by iteratively following degree-2 nodes starting from a leaf of ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}; this path satisfies the following property:

Observation 3.

For any path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, all piece sides corresponding to the nodes along the path have equal lengths.

3.2 Vertex Matching Diagram

Next, we consider the relationships between the corners of the pieces and the vertices of the cut graph. This relationship can be considered more simply compared to the relationships between edges discussed in Section 3.1. A corner of a piece corresponds to a vertex in the cut graph GXG^{X} of each target shape X∈{P,P′}X\in\{P,P^{\prime}\}. Conversely, when looking at the vertices of GXG^{X}, one or multiple piece corners may gather. To capture this relationship, we introduce the following definition:

Definition 4.

We define a vertex matching diagram 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} for GPG^{P} and GP′G^{P^{\prime}} (see Figure 5):

  • •

    For each X∈{P,P′}X\in\{P,P^{\prime}\}, define the node set NX​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{X}(\mathscr{VD}) as V⁡(GX)V(G^{X}).

  • •

    Let L⁡(𝒱​𝒟)L(\mathscr{VD}) be the set of links between NP​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{P}(\mathscr{VD}) and NP′​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{P^{\prime}}(\mathscr{VD}) by connecting a link for each corner x∈V⁡(P1)∪V⁡(P2)∪⋯∪V⁡(Pk)x\in V(P_{1})\cup V(P_{2})\cup\cdots\cup V(P_{k}) according to the correspondence between links representing the corners of pieces and nodes representing the vertices of the graph.

Since each node of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} corresponds to a vertex of the cut graph, we define the terms corner, side, paired, convex, reflex, and flat directly for the nodes as well.

We define a weight ω⁡(x)\omega(x) for each node xx of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} by the sum of the interior angles of the corners that gather at vv. The value of ω⁡(x)\omega(x) is 2​π2\pi if xx is a paired, convex, or reflex vertex. In the case that xx is a flat or side node, ω⁡(x)\omega(x) is π\pi. In the case that xx is a corner node, ω⁡(x)\omega(x) is the interior angle of the corresponding corner of the target shape.

We can also observe the following by the fact that a paired vertex, which is shared by two corners, has a weight of 2​π2\pi:

Observation 5.

For any path in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} that consists of paired vertices, ∠⁡(x)+∠⁡(x′)=2​π\angle(x)+\angle(x^{\prime})=2\pi or ∠⁡(x)=∠⁡(x′)\angle(x)=\angle(x^{\prime}) holds depending on whether the length of the path is odd or even, where xx and x′x^{\prime} are the corners corresponding to the endpoint nodes of the path.

Taking the union of the piece vertices gathered at each node sets NP​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{P}(\mathscr{VD}) and NP′​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{P^{\prime}}(\mathscr{VD}), we can count the piece vertex set in two different ways, revealing the following fact:

Observation 6.

Any connected component CC of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} satisfies

∑x∈N⁡(C)∩NP​(𝒱​𝒟)ω⁡(x)=∑x∈N⁡(C)∩NP′​(𝒱​𝒟)ω⁡(x).\sum_{x\in N(C)\cap N^{P}(\mathscr{VD})}\omega(x)=\sum_{x\in N(C)\cap N^{P^{\prime}}(\mathscr{VD})}\omega(x).

3.3 Relationship between Vertex and Edge Matching Diagrams

This section describes the relationship between paths in the edge and vertex matching diagram, which are generated by sides and their endpoint corners. Formally, when a side of a piece is placed along the horizontal axis with the inside of the piece facing downward, the corner on the right is referred to as clockwise next, while the one on the left is referred to as counterclockwise next. The same definitions apply to the corners as viewed from a side.

The following lemma describes the relationship between a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, starting from a side, and the 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} path formed by the corners that come next along the boundary of the target shape.

Lemma 7.

Let ee and e′e^{\prime} be links in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, that is, sides of pieces, and assume that they are connected by a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}. Let v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} be the clockwise and counterclockwise next corners of ee, respectively. Similarly, define v1′v^{\prime}_{1} and v2′v^{\prime}_{2} for e′e^{\prime}. Here, v1v_{1} is connected to either v1′v^{\prime}_{1} or v2′v^{\prime}_{2} by a path in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}, and v2v_{2} is connected to the other.

Proof.

Based on the assumption that ee and e′e^{\prime} are connected by a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, each node along this path corresponds to a one-to-one pairing of two sides of the pieces. Since these two sides form an a single edge of the cut graph, the vertices at both endpoints of this edge correspond to the corners of the respective sides. Therefore, there exists a pair of paths in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} that shares a node between the pairs of corners to which the two next sides correspond. ∎

Note that which pair corresponds depends on whether the piece is flipped or not. When any piece is not flipped, it is possible to precisely describe which pair corresponds. This will be discussed in Section 3.4.

Next, we consider the relationship between a 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} path and the ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} paths formed by the next sides of the corner in the 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} path. Before describing this relationship, we define some terminology. Let us consider a paired vertex xx of GXG^{X} such that both adjacent vertices are non-flat. In this case, pairs of the next sides of the corner corresponding to xx create degree-2 nodes in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} (see the left of Figure 7). On the other hand, in other cases—such as when xx is a corner vertex, a side vertex, a flat vertex, or a paired vertex adjacent to a flat vertex—one pair of sides does not correspond to each other and remain as degree-1 nodes, while the other pair corresponds to a degree-2 node (see the middle of Figure 7). In particular, when passing through a side vertex that bisects a side ee of a piece, the sum of the lengths of the disconnected paths is equal to the length of ee (see the right of Figure 7).

Based on these observations, we introduce the following definition:

Definition 8.

We introduce the following notations (see Figure 8):

  • •

    N𝑑𝑖𝑡X​(𝒱​𝒟)⊂NX​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{X}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD})\subset N^{X}(\mathscr{VD}) denotes the union of side vertices whose adjacent vertices are both corner vertices and of flat vertices whose adjacent vertices are both paired vertices. These are referred to as divide-in-two vertices.

  • •

    N𝑏𝑢𝑟X​(𝒱​𝒟)⊂NX​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{X}_{\mathit{bur}}(\mathscr{VD})\subset N^{X}(\mathscr{VD}) denotes the set of paired vertices such that both adjacent vertices are non-flat. These are referred to as buried vertices.

Then, a path P=(p1,…,pk)P=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{k}) of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} is well-behaved if p2,…,pk−1∈N𝑑𝑖𝑡X​(𝒱​𝒟)∪N𝑏𝑢𝑟X​(𝒱​𝒟)p_{2},\ldots,p_{k-1}\in N^{X}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD})\cup N^{X}_{\mathit{bur}}(\mathscr{VD}).

Using the above definition, the relationship between a 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} path and its adjacent ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} paths can be expressed by the following lemma:

Lemma 9.

Let PP be a well-behaved path in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}, vv be an end node of PP, and ee be the next side of vv. We define an along sequence M1,…,MkM_{1},\ldots,M_{k} of paths in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} as follows:

  • •

    Each MjM_{j} is a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, and the end node of M1M_{1} is ee.

  • •

    A pair of adjacent edges—one ending MjM_{j} and the other starting Mj+1M_{j+1}—share a point in N𝑑𝑖𝑡X​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{X}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) on a side LiL_{i} as one of their end nodes.

Then, the alternating sum of |e|,|L1|,|L2|,…,|e′||e|,|L_{1}|,|L_{2}|,\ldots,|e^{\prime}| is zero where e′e^{\prime} is the end node of MkM_{k}.

Proof.

The side ee and part of L1L_{1} share a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, and according to Observation 3, their lengths are equal. Moreover, the remaining part of L1L_{1} and part of L2L_{2} also share a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, and these lengths are equal as well. The equality of all these parts implies that the alternating sum of the lengths is zero. ∎

3.4 Lemmas when Flipping is not Allowed

When flipping of a piece is not allowed, the relationship between the connected components in Lemma 7 can be described based on the length of the paths as follows:

Lemma 10.

We use the same notation as in Lemma 7. Let C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} be connected components of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}, where v1∈C1v_{1}\in C_{1} and v2∈C2v_{2}\in C_{2}.

  • •

    If the length of PP is odd, then v2′∈C1v^{\prime}_{2}\in C_{1} and v1′∈C2v^{\prime}_{1}\in C_{2}.

  • •

    If the length of PP is even, then v1′∈C1v^{\prime}_{1}\in C_{1} and v2′∈C2v^{\prime}_{2}\in C_{2}.

Proof.

This can be easily verified by observing that when two pieces share a side and come into contact, the clockwise-next corner on one piece corresponds to the counterclockwise-next corner on the other(Figure 10). ∎

In addition, Lemma 10 leads to the following lemma, which helps to simplify our proof:

Lemma 11.

Let ee and e′e^{\prime} be boundary edges of GXG^{X} such that they share an endpoint vv. If ee and e′e^{\prime} are connected by a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, the connected component of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} that includes vv contains a cycle.

Proof.

By Lemma 10, if ee and e′e^{\prime} are connected by a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, we can trace a path in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} that begins and ends at vv (Figure 11). This implies that the component containing vv includes a cycle. ∎

In particular, we use these lemmas in combination as follows:

Lemma 12.

Let CC be a connected component of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} that contains a boundary node vv, and suppose the following conditions hold:

  • •

    Both of the next sides ss and s′s^{\prime} of vv along the boundary correspond to monochromatic nodes in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}.

  • •

    None of the next sides of any other node in CC correspond to monochromatic nodes in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}.

Then CC forms a cycle.

4 Proof Overview and Example

In this section, we provide an overview of how to prove the impossibility. We let PP be a square SS and P′P^{\prime} be an equilateral triangle TT. We denote the side lengths of SS and TT by σ\sigma and τ\tau, respectively, and set σ=3\sigma=\sqrt{\sqrt{3}} and τ=2\tau=2 so that both areas are 3\sqrt{3}.

First, in Section 5.1, we consider the equivalence classes of the cut graph under the equivalence relation ∼\sim. Although this is essentially a brute-force exhaustive search, several tools are introduced to help to reduce the number of case distinctions. Next, in Section 5.2, we perform a more detailed analysis of the properties that hold for matching diagrams when considering equilateral triangles and squares. Finally, in Section 5.3, using these tools, we complete the proof by deriving contradictions for each individual case.

In the following, we present an example of the proof method by borrowing some tools in advance. We focus on the case where representative elements of equivalence classes GTG^{T} and GSG^{S} are the cut graphs shown on the left of Figure 12. This pair of cut graphs corresponds to G𝔇​1T{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}} and G𝔄​3S{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}3}} in the later labeling. the same proof also applies to G𝔇​1T{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}} and G𝔇​7S{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}7}}.

Lemma 13.

The combination of G𝔇​1T{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}} and G𝔄​3S{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}3}} is infeasible.

Proof.

In this case, by Lemma 21, which will be given later, 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} contains, as a connected component, a tree YY that connects each corner of TT and a degree-3 vertex qq by a well-behaved path. Let vxv_{x}, vyv_{y}, and vzv_{z} be the three leaves of YY, with the adjacent sides of vxv_{x} being x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}, those of vyv_{y} being y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}, and those of vzv_{z} being z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} (see the middle of Figure 12). Here, the sides x1x_{1}, x2x_{2}, y1y_{1}, y2y_{2}, z1z_{1}, and z2z_{2} can be grouped into three pairs, each pair forming a side of TT. Therefore, one of the following holds (see the right of Figure 12):

  • •

    Equation 1: ‖x1‖+‖y2‖=‖y1‖+‖z2‖=‖z1‖+|x2|=τ\|x_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\|y_{1}\|+\|z_{2}\|=\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\tau.

  • •

    Equation 2: ‖x1‖+‖z2‖=‖y1‖+‖x2‖=‖z1‖+|y2|=τ\|x_{1}\|+\|z_{2}\|=\|y_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\|z_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\tau.

Let WxW_{x}, WyW_{y}, and WzW_{z} be the paths in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} between each leaf and qq. We consider the number of points from N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) and N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) included in each W−W_{-}. Since the vertices vxv_{x}, vyv_{y}, vzv_{z}, and the convex vertex qq are all included in GTG^{T}, the weight of both endpoint nodes of each W−W_{-} is at most π\pi. By Observation 6, each W−W_{-} contains at least one node of N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}). Moreover, since the weight of a divide-in-two vertex is π\pi, the elements of N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) appear alternately with those of N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}), and the number of N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) contained is one less than the number of N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}). Therefore, since ‖N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)‖=4\|N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD})\|=4, the number of elements from N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) in each path is 11 or 22, and the number from N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) is 00 or 11. If YY includes a point in N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}), it is a side vertex of GTG^{T}.

If YY includes exactly one side vertex tt, then the only monochromatic sides connected to YY are the two adjacent to tt. Therefore, the connected component including tt must contain a cycle by Lemma 12, contradicting the fact that YY is a tree.

Next, we consider the case where YY includes no side vertex of TT. In this case, there are two possible structures for YY, as shown in Figure 13. Depending on whether we are considering the left or right case in Figure 13, by Lemma 9, we have one of the following:

  • •

    Equations A: ‖x1‖+‖y2‖=σ\|x_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\sigma,  ‖y1‖+‖z2‖=σ\|y_{1}\|+\|z_{2}\|=\sigma,  ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma.

  • •

    Equations B: ‖x1‖=‖y2‖\|x_{1}\|=\|y_{2}\|,  ‖y1‖=‖z2‖\|y_{1}\|=\|z_{2}\|,  ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma.

Here, even if YY contains a flat node, by Lemma 20, which will be shown later, the length of the side of the piece being divided is σ\sigma.

From Equations A and Equation 1 or 2, we derive ‖x1‖+‖x2‖+‖y1‖+‖y2​‖+‖z1‖+‖​z2‖=3​σ=3​τ,\|x_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|+\|y_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|+\|z_{1}\|+\|z_{2}\|=3\sigma=3\tau, which contradicts σ≠τ\sigma\neq\tau. From Equations B and Equation 1, we have ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma and ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=τ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\tau, which is a contradiction. From Equations B and Equation 2, we have ‖z1‖+‖y2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\sigma and ‖z1‖+‖y2‖=τ\|z_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\tau, which is also a contradiction.

∎

5 Main Proof

In this section, we give the proof of Theorem 1.

5.1 Enumeration of Patterns of Cut Graphs

In this section, we enumerate the equivalence classes of the equivalence relation ∼\sim. Before the enumeration, we present several geometric lemmas.

5.1.1 Geometric Lemma for Cut Graphs

Lemma 14.

In any dissection of TT and SS, no piece contains two corners of TT. Thus, the number of pieces must be at least 33, and in a three-piece dissection P1,P2,P3P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}, each PiP_{i} contains exactly one corner of TT.

Proof.

Suppose a piece contains two corners of TT, whose Euclidean distance is τ=2\tau=2. The longest distance between any two points in SS is 2​3\sqrt{2\sqrt{3}}, so no piece contains points that are farther apart than this distance. Since 2​3<2\sqrt{2\sqrt{3}}<2, we obtain a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 15.

Let P1,P2,P3P_{1},P_{2},P_{3} be a three-piece dissection of TT and SS. Then no PiP_{i} contains two diagonal corners of SS.

Proof.

If a single piece PiP_{i} contains the diagonal corners of SS, the diameter of PiP_{i} is 2​3\sqrt{2\sqrt{3}}. Placing a line segment dd of this length 2​3\sqrt{2\sqrt{3}} in TT requires its endpoints to reside within the region in TT bounded by the two blue parallel lines shown in Figure 14. By Lemma 14, piece PiP_{i} must also include exactly one corner vv of TT. Since the line segment dd must be a diameter of PiP_{i}, dd must in fact have vv as an endpoint. Limited by the region, dd must form an angle of more than π4\frac{\pi}{4} with an edge of TT (the horizontal edge in Figure 14). However in SS, the diagonal has only π4\frac{\pi}{4} of material on either side of its endpoints. Thus, PiP_{i} cannot fully cover the corner vv of TT, i.e., vv is in fact cut. This contradicts Lemma 14. ∎

Lemma 16.

Let P1,P2,P3P_{1},P_{2},P_{3} be a three-piece dissection of TT and SS. Then we can assume without loss of generality that each PiP_{i} is a simple polygon.

Proof.

By Lemmas 14 and 15, the boundary of each polygon must be cut at least twice. Thus, under the assumption of a three-piece dissection, the number of holes in a single piece is at most one, and its interior must be filled by exactly one other piece. In this case (right of Figure 15), we can remove the cycle to obtain a dissection with fewer pieces. Similarly, if the dissection includes cut lines whose endpoints are internal (left of Figure 15), we can remove these cuts while maintaining the same number of pieces. Thus, in either case, we obtain a dissection with the same or smaller number of pieces that are all simple. ∎

5.1.2 Procedure for Enumerating Cut Graphs

We classify the possible equivalence classes of the relation ∼\sim using Lemmas 14, 15, and 16.

We begin by abstracting the boundary of the target shape as a disk, ignoring differences in vertex types. First, consider the case of partitioning the disk into two pieces. Since each piece must be a simple polygon (by Lemma 16), the boundary must be cut at least once. As shown on the left of Figure 17, there is a unique way to perform such a cut: connect two points on the circular boundary with a cut line CC. The resulting boundary of the pieces consists of three types of segments: parts from the cut line CC, parts from the original boundary, and two switching points between them.

To obtain three pieces, we make a second cut C′C^{\prime} on one of the two pieces, again connecting two boundary points. As shown on the right of Figure 17, there are exactly six distinct ways to make such a second cut. These yield six topologically distinct configurations, which we enumerate explicitly in Figure 17 and label as Type 𝔄\mathfrak{A} through Type 𝔉\mathfrak{F}.

We now apply this abstract classification to the actual dissection of the target shapes SS and TT. To do so, we must account for how the endpoints of each cut line attach to the corners or sides of the target shape, as well as the presence of vertices of degree three or higher. Using Lemma 14, we enumerate the equivalence classes of GTG^{T} as shown in Figure 18, denoting them as GiTG^{T}_{i}.

Similarly, applying Lemma 15, we enumerate the equivalence classes of GSG^{S} as shown in Figures 19 and 20, denoted as GjSG^{S}_{j}.

To identify feasible pairings between G−SG^{S}_{-} and G−TG^{T}_{-}, we introduce the following angular invariant:

5.2 Lemmas for Equilateral Triangle and Square

In this section, we present two lemmas that are useful in proving properties related to the dissection between an equilateral triangle and a square.

The first lemma constrains on the structure of the connected components of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} and can be described as follows:

Lemma 18.

Any connected component of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} includes either all corner vertices of TT or none, and includes an even number of corner vertices of SS.

Proof.

Except for the corner vertices of SS and TT, the weight of any vertex is a multiple of π\pi (see Figure 21). Therefore, if the conditions in the statement do not hold, the sums on both sides will not match. It contradicts to Observation 6. ∎

The second lemma is used to handle well-behavior properties. When dealing with the 3-piece dissection between an equilateral triangle and a square, a path ceases to be well-behaved when it passes through a corner vertex, a vertex adjacent to a flat vertex, or a side vertex located on a trisected edge of the target shape. Here, in addition to the node in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} added for an edge containing a flat node, we also define the node corresponding to the middle of a trisected side as a trisected-mid node. Thus, to verify that a path is well-behaved, it is sufficient to check that it does not pass through a corner vertex and does not go through the endpoints of a flat node or a trisected-mid node. Regarding the behavior of flat nodes and trisected-mid nodes in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, the following holds:

Definition 19.

Let ee be a boundary edge of GSG^{S} and v,v′v,v^{\prime} be the adjacent vertices of xx. (v,e,v′)(v,e,v^{\prime}) is called a U-shaped boundary if both vv and v′v^{\prime} are a corner vertex of degree 1 in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}.

Lemma 20.

Assume that (v,e,v′)(v,e,v^{\prime}) forms a U-shaped boundary and that the connected components containing vv and v′v^{\prime} (which may be the same) are both simple paths. Then, the other end node e′e^{\prime} of the path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} with ee as an end node is either a flat node or a trisected-mid node in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}.

Proof.

Let W=(v,v1,…,vk)W=(v,v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}) and W′=(v′,v1′,…,vk′′)W^{\prime}=(v^{\prime},v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}) be the paths in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} beginning from vv and v′v^{\prime}, respectively.

First, we show that for each of the sequences v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1} and v1′,…,vk′−1′v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}-1}, at least one element in each sequence is either a flat vertex or a boundary vertex of SS or TT. It suffices to show this for v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1}. Suppose, for contradiction, that all v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1} are paired vertices. Then, by Lemma 5, ∠​vk\angle{v_{k}} would be either π/2\pi/2 or 3​π/23\pi/2, depending on whether vk∈NT​(𝒱​𝒟)v_{k}\in N^{T}(\mathscr{VD}) or vk∈NS​(𝒱​𝒟)v_{k}\in N^{S}(\mathscr{VD}). However, since vkv_{k} is an endpoint of the path, it must be a corner vertex of X∈{S,T}X\in\{S,T\}. In the case of TT, the internal angle at vkv_{k} would be π/3\pi/3, and in the case of SS, it would be π/2\pi/2, leading to a contradiction.

Therefore, both v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1} and v1′,…,vk′−1′v^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}-1} must contain at least one flat vertex or boundary vertex of SS or TT. Let ss and s′s^{\prime} be the first such points encountered along WW and W′W^{\prime} from vv and v′v^{\prime}, respectively. By Lemma 5, both ss and s′s^{\prime} must belong to NT​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}(\mathscr{VD}). Now, assume for contradiction that the statement of the lemma does not hold. Suppose that e′e^{\prime} is neither a flat node nor trisected-mid node. Then, e′e^{\prime} cannot have ss (or s′s^{\prime}) as its adjacent side. If it did, the other endpoint of e′e^{\prime} would be a corner tt of TT, and tt and s′s^{\prime} (or ss) would be connected in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}, which contradicts the fact that W′W^{\prime} (or WW) is a path and Lemma 18. Therefore, at both ss and s′s^{\prime}, the path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} starting from ee has degree-2 and corresponds to cut lines of length σ\sigma perpendicular to a side of SS at both ss and s′s^{\prime}. If the cut lines attached to ss and s′s^{\prime} are the same, this would imply that TT has a pair of parallel sides on its boundary (right of Figure 22), leading to a contradiction. On the other hand, if the cut lines attached to ss and s′s^{\prime} are different, this implies the existence of a pair of cut lines of length σ\sigma orthogonal to the sides of TT, which intersect within TT (left of Figure 22), leading to another contradiction.

In the case where WW and W′W^{\prime} are the same path, it is possible that ss and s′s^{\prime} are the same vertex. However, this would mean that the endpoint of the path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} that starts at ee would be ee itself, contradicting the definition of a path. ∎

5.3 Proofs for Individual Cases

In this section, we apply the approach to eliminate the remaining cases narrowed down in Section 5.1. Rather than deriving a classification from abstract principles, we arrived at a practical case division through extensive trial-and-error analysis of all surviving cut graphs. Based on recurring structural features, we group the configurations into three representative types, which we refer to as Cases A, B, and C. Each of these captures a common geometric obstruction, and together they account for all infeasible instances identified in the enumeration. We begin by formulating Lemma 21 that justifies this trichotomy.

Lemma 21.

We define Cases A, B, and C as follows:

  • •

    Case A: {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔇​6S,G𝔉​1S,G𝔉​2S,G𝔉​4S,G𝔉​11S,G𝔉​3S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}1},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}2},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}4},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}11},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}3}\}, {G𝔇​2T,G𝔉​1T}×{G𝔅​2S.G𝔈​1S,G𝔈​3S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}2},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{F}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}2}.G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}1},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}3}\}, {G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔉​8S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}8}\}

    Case B: {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔄​3S,G𝔇​7S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}7}\}, {G𝔇​2T,G𝔉​1T}×{G𝔈​2S,G𝔈​4S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}2},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{F}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}2},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}4}\}

  • •

    Case C: {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔄​4S,G𝔅​1S,G𝔇​3S,G𝔇​4S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}4},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}1},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}4}\}, {G𝔇​2T,G𝔉​1T}×{G𝔇​5S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}2},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{F}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}5}\}, {G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔄​6S,G𝔅​3S,Gℭ​1S,G𝔇​10S,G𝔇​13S,G𝔇​14S,G𝔈​5S,G𝔈​6S,G𝔈​7S,G𝔉​10S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}6},\allowbreak G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}3},\allowbreak G^{S}_{\mathfrak{C}1},\allowbreak G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}10},\allowbreak G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}13},\allowbreak G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}14},\allowbreak G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}5},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}6},\allowbreak G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}7},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}10}\}

In Case A (Figure 23), the number of flat edges and the middle of trisected edges of SS or TT is less than the number of U-shaped boundaries. In Case B (Figure 24), there exists a well-behaved tree YY of ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} that connects a degree-33 vertex and each corners of TT by a well-behaved path. In Case C (Figure 25), there exists a well-behaved path WW that connects vertices of SS.

Proof.

In Case A, the statement clearly holds.

In Case B, by Lemma 18, the connected components of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} consist of a tree YY connecting the corners of TT and paths W1W_{1} and W2W_{2} connecting the corners of SS, since there is a single vertex of degree 3 of GSG^{S} and GTG^{T}. According to Lemma 20, the paths in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} starting from the edges of the U-shaped boundary have either a flat node or a trisected-mid node as an endpoint. Thus, the adjacent vertices belong to either W1W_{1} or W2W_{2}. Consequently, all three paths composing YY are well-behaved.

In Case C, there are at most three vertices of degree 3 in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}, and the number of leaves in a connected component is at most five. Therefore, by Lemma 18, 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} must include a connected component that forms a path WW connecting a pair of corners of SS. It is clear that WW is well-behaved in the combinations {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔄​4S,G𝔅​1S,G𝔇​3S,G𝔇​4S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}4},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}1},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}4}\} and {G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔄​6S,G𝔅​3S,Gℭ​1S,G𝔇​13S,G𝔇​14S,G𝔈​5S,G𝔈​6S,G𝔈​7S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{C}1},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}13},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}14},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}5},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}7}\}, since by Observation 5, WW does not pass through corner vertices of SS with degree greater than two. Now, we consider the remaining cases of {G𝔇​2T,G𝔉​1T}×{G𝔇​5S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}2},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{F}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}5}\} and {G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​10S,G𝔉​10S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}10},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}10}\}. Let ee be the side of SS whose both corners have degree greater than 2 in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}. Since ee is monochromatic, any edge e′e^{\prime} sharing a path with ee in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} is also monochromatic. If e′e^{\prime} is a flat node or a trisected-mid node, WW does not pass through these endpoints, making it well-behaved. If e′e^{\prime} is an edge bisecting an side of TT, then any edge e′′e^{\prime\prime} sharing this edge with e′e^{\prime} is also monochromatic. By following paths in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} recursively, we eventually reach a flat node or a trisected-mid node, which is also monochromatic. Thus, WW does not pass through these vertices, making it well-behaved. ∎

The structural property established in the above lemma allows us to rule out each of the remaining cases. We now examine them one by one.

Lemma 22.

Case A is infeasible.

Proof.

Each Case A pattern contains a single vertex of degree 3, and the three corners of TT are connected by a tree YY that includes this degree-3 vertex. Therefore, the corners of SS on the U-shaped boundary (v,e,v′)(v,e,v^{\prime}) are both included in paths of 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}.

By Lemma 20, the other endpoint of the path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} starting from ee must be either a flat node or a trisected-mid node. Furthermore, by Lemma 21, the number of such edges is smaller than the number of U-shaped boundaries. This leads to a contradiction, proving that Case A is infeasible. ∎

Lemma 23.

Case B is infeasible.

Proof.

In this case, there exists a well-behaved tree YY by Lemma 21. Let WxW_{x}, WyW_{y}, and WzW_{z} be the paths in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} between each leaf and qq. Let vxv_{x}, vyv_{y}, and vzv_{z} be the three leaves of YY with the sides next to vxv_{x} being x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}, those connected to vyv_{y} being y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}, and those connected to vzv_{z} being z1z_{1} and z2z_{2}. Here, the sides x1x_{1}, x2x_{2}, y1y_{1}, y2y_{2}, z1z_{1}, and z2z_{2} can be grouped into three pairs, each pair forming a side of TT.

Therefore, one of the following holds (see the left of Figure 12):

  • •

    Equation 1: x1+y2=y1+z2=z1+x2=τx_{1}+y_{2}=y_{1}+z_{2}=z_{1}+x_{2}=\tau.

  • •

    Equation 2: x1+z2=y1+x2=z1+y2=τx_{1}+z_{2}=y_{1}+x_{2}=z_{1}+y_{2}=\tau.

We now consider two cases based on the location of the degree-3 vertex qq of YY: in Case B-1, qq belongs to GTG^{T}, while in Case B-2, it belongs to GSG^{S}.

Case B-1: The degree-3 vertex qq is in GTG^{T}: This proof is a repetition of Section 4. We analyze the number of points from N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) and N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) included in each W−W_{-}. Since the vertices vxv_{x}, vyv_{y}, vzv_{z} and the convex vertex qq are all included in GTG^{T}, the weight of both endpoint nodes of each W−W_{-} is at most π\pi. By Observation 6, each W−W_{-} contains at least one node of N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}), and the number of N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) is one less than that of N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}). Since ‖N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)‖≤4\|N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD})\|\leq 4, each path contains at most two elements from N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}) and at most one from N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}). If YY includes a point in N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}), it must be a side vertex of GTG^{T}.

We now analyze how many side vertices are included in YY. If YY includes exactly one side vertex tt, then the only monochromatic sides connected to YY are the two adjacent to tt. Therefore, the connected component including tt must contain a cycle by Lemma 12, contradicting the fact that YY is a tree. If YY includes no side vertex of TT, then its structure must be one of the two cases shown in Figure 13. By Lemma 9, we obtain the following equations:

  • •

    Equations A: ‖x1‖+‖y2‖=σ\|x_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\sigma,  ‖y1‖+‖z2‖=σ\|y_{1}\|+\|z_{2}\|=\sigma,  ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma.

  • •

    Equations B: ‖x1‖=‖y2‖\|x_{1}\|=\|y_{2}\|,  ‖y1‖=‖z2‖\|y_{1}\|=\|z_{2}\|,  ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma.

Here, even if YY contains a flat node, Lemma 20 implies that the side of the piece being divided has length σ\sigma. From Equations A, we derive:

‖x1‖+‖x2‖+‖y1‖+‖y2‖+‖z1‖+|z2|=3​σ,\|x_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|+\|y_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|+\|z_{1}\|+\|z_{2}\|=3\sigma,

which contradicts Equation 1 and 2 since σ≠τ\sigma\neq\tau. Similarly, Equations B also contradicts Equation 1 and 2. Specifically, when Equations B and Equation 1 hold, we have ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma and ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=τ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\tau, which is a contradiction. When Equations B and Equation 2 hold, we have ‖z1‖+‖y2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\sigma and ‖z1‖+‖y2‖=τ\|z_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\tau, which is also a contradiction.

Case B-2: The degree-3 vertex qq is in GSG^{S}: Here, qq is a boundary vertex, and the divided sides are denoted as e1e_{1} and e2e_{2}. Let f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} be their respective endpoints. Without loss of generality, we assume that x2x_{2} and e1e_{1}, z1z_{1} and e2e_{2}, x1x_{1} and y2y_{2}, and y1y_{1} and z2z_{2} share along paths. Since qq is in GSG^{S}, all surrounding angles are less than π\pi, and each W−W_{-} contains at least one non-paired node. The first non-paired node encountered is either qq or an element of N𝑑𝑖𝑡S​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{S}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}).

If YY includes two side nodes tt and t′t^{\prime} on sides of TT, then WxW_{x} and WzW_{z} contain monochromatic edges. Since at least one of vx,vyv_{x},v_{y}, and vzv_{z} is adjacent to monochromatic edges on both sides (specifically, vyv_{y}), WyW_{y} contains no vertex on edges of TT. The possible structures are shown in Figure 26. Depending on whether we are considering the left or right case in the figure, by Lemma 9, we have one of the following:

  • •

    Equations C: ‖x1‖=‖y2‖\|x_{1}\|=\|y_{2}\|,  ‖y1‖=‖z2‖\|y_{1}\|=\|z_{2}\|,  ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma.

  • •

    Equations D: ‖x1‖+‖y2‖=τ\|x_{1}\|+\|y_{2}\|=\tau,  ‖y1‖+‖z2‖=τ\|y_{1}\|+\|z_{2}\|=\tau,  ‖z1‖+‖x2‖=σ\|z_{1}\|+\|x_{2}\|=\sigma.

Equations C are equivalent to Equations B, and Equations D lead to |x1|+|x2|+|y1|+|y2|+|z1|+|z2|=2​τ+σ|x_{1}|+|x_{2}|+|y_{1}|+|y_{2}|+|z_{1}|+|z_{2}|=2\tau+\sigma. Therefore, both contradict Equation 1 and Equation 2.

If YY includes one side node tt of TT, the only monochromatic edges connected to YY are the two adjacent to tt. These edges should be connected via paths in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, contradicting Corollary 11.

Finally, if YY includes no side node of TT, then YY contains at most one vertex from N𝑑𝑖𝑡T​(𝒱​𝒟)N^{T}_{\mathit{dit}}(\mathscr{VD}), which is a flat node. By Lemma 20, the side length of the divided piece must be σ\sigma. Consequently, the possible patterns are the seven shown in Figure 27. This again leads to Equations A or B, contradicting Equation 1 and 2.

∎

Lemma 24.

Case C is infeasible.

Proof.

We classify the cases as follows:

  • •

    Case C-1: {G𝔇​2T,G𝔉​1T}×{G𝔇​5S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​10S,G𝔉​10S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}2},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{F}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}5}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}10},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}10}\}

  • •

    Case C-2: {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔄​4S,G𝔅​1S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔄​6S,G𝔅​3S,Gℭ​1S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}4},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}1}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{C}1}\}

  • •

    Case C-3: {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔇​3S,G𝔇​4S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​13S,G𝔇​14S,G𝔈​5S,G𝔈​6S,G𝔈​7S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}4}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}13},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}14},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}5},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}7}\}

By Lemmas 21 and 18, the structure of the connected components in each case can be classified as follows:

  • •

    Case C-1:

    • –

      A well-behaved path WW and a tree YY with a degree-3 vertex.

  • •

    Case C-2:

    • –

      A well-behaved path W1W_{1}, a path W2W_{2}, and some component CC, or

    • –

      A well-behaved path W1W_{1} and some component CC.

  • •

    Case C-3:

    • –

      A well-behaved path WW, a tadpole graph LL, which is a graph obtained by joining a cycle graph to a path graph with a bridge of degree 3, and a tree YY with a degree-3 vertex, or

    • –

      A well-behaved path WW and a tree YY with a degree-4 vertex.

Case C-1: {G𝔇​2T,G𝔉​1T}×{G𝔇​5S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​10S,G𝔉​10S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}2},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{F}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}5}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}10},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}10}\}: As shown in the proof of Lemma 21, the node in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} that shares a path with the side of SS where both adjacent corners have degree-2 in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} must be either a trisected-mid node or a flat node. In G𝔉​10SG^{S}_{\mathfrak{F}10}, the trisected-mid node lies on the side of SS, however its length is strictly shorter than the side length of SS, leading to a contradiction. Thus, we only consider G𝔇​5SG^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}5} and G𝔇​10SG^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}10}. Since the endpoints ww and w′w^{\prime} of WW are corner vertices of SS, if WW contains a divide-in-two vertex tt on the side of SS, only the two next sides of tt become monochromatic (Figure 28). This contradicts Lemma 12. Thus, we only consider the case where WW does not contain a divide-in-two vertex on the side of SS.

Case C-1-1: {G𝔇​2T,G𝔉​1T}×{G𝔇​5S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}2},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{F}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}5}\}: Since WW does not contain a divide-in-two vertex on the side of SS, there is exactly one divide-in-two vertex on the side of TT contained in WW. Thus, the structure of WW must be one of the two cases shown in Figure 29. In these cases, one of the along sequences consists of a single path, while the other consists of two paths. According to Lemma 9, the sum of the lengths of the paths in the along sequence consisting of two paths should equal τ\tau. However, the length of the counterclockwise-next side of ww and clockwise-next side of w′w^{\prime} are both σ\sigma, and the sum of the lengths of the clockwise next side of ww and the counterclockwise next side of w′w^{\prime} is also σ\sigma. As a result, it is impossible for either sum to be τ\tau, leading to a contradiction.

Case C-1-2: {G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​10S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}10}\}: Since WW does not contain a divide-in-two vertex on the side of SS, WW either contains only one divide-in-two vertex on the side of TT, or it contains one flat vertex on SS and two divide-in-two vertices on the side of TT. In the former case, a contradiction arises in the same way as in Case C-1-1. In the latter case, the remaining boundary vertex tt on TT that is not contained in WW is contained in YY. (There is no divide-in-two vertex on SS that is not contained in WW, so tt cannot be part of a cycle.) Since tt is contained in YY, only its next side becomes monochromatic, which contradicts Lemma 12 (Figure 30).

Case C-2: {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔄​4S,G𝔅​1S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔄​6S,G𝔅​3S,Gℭ​1S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}4},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}1}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{A}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{B}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{C}1}\}: If 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} has two separate paths W1W_{1} and W2W_{2}, a contradiction arises by Lemma 20. Therefore, we consider the case where there is only one path WW contained in 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD}. By Lemma 20, it suffices to consider the case where the endpoints ww and w′w^{\prime} of WW belong to different U-shaped boundaries. There are two possibilities: either ww and w′w^{\prime} are diagonal corners of SS, or ww and w′w^{\prime} are the endpoint corners of a single side of SS.

Case C-2-1: the case where ww and w′w^{\prime} are diagonal corners of SS: If WW contains a divide-in-two node on the side of SS, it contradicts Lemma 12 (see the left of Figure 31). Conversely, if WW does not contain a divide-in-two node on the side of SS, the structure of WW must be one of the two cases shown in the right of Figure 31. In both cases, one of the along sequences of WW forms a single path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}, however the next sides of ww and w′w^{\prime} in different directions have different lengths, leading to a contradiction to Observation 3.

Case C-2-2: the case where ww and w′w^{\prime} are the endpoint corners of a single side of SS: If WW contains two divide-in-two nodes on SS, one of them divides the side whose endpoints are the corner vertices ww and w′w^{\prime}. The boundary edges corresponding to the divided side are both monochromatic, which contradicts Lemma 12. For the other cases, where WW contains at most one divide-in-two node on SS, a contradiction arises in the same way as in Case C-1-2.

Case C-3: {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔇​3S,G𝔇​4S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​13S,G𝔇​14S,G𝔈​5S,G𝔈​6S,G𝔈​7S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}4}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}13},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}14},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}5},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}7}\}: If 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} contains a tadpole graph LL, then the degree-2 corner vertex of SS (along with one of the degree-1 corner vertices) is included in LL, and the tree YY is well-behaved. In this case, a contradiction arises using the same argument as in Case B. Therefore, we focus on the scenario where 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} consists of a well-behaved path WW and a tree YY with a degree-4 vertex. In each case, there exist two sides that are not divided by a side vertex, which we denote as ee and e′e^{\prime}.

Case C-3-1: the case where ee and e′e^{\prime} are connected by a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}: In the cases of {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔇​4S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​14S,G𝔈​5S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}4}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}14},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}5}\}, Lemma 10 implies that a degree-2 corner vertex is included in a cycle, contradicting the fact that 𝒱​𝒟\mathscr{VD} does not contain a tadpole graph. In other cases, such as {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔇​3S},{G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​13S,G𝔈​6S,G𝔈​7S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}3}\},\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}13},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}6},G^{S}_{\mathfrak{E}7}\}, computing the along sequence of WW on the side that is not ee, regardless of the number of divide-in-two vertices contained in WW, leads to a contradiction with Lemma 9.

Case C-3-2: the case where ee and e′e^{\prime} are not connected by a path in ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED}: Since ee and e′e^{\prime} both have a length of σ\sigma, the other endpoints of the ℰ​𝒟\mathscr{ED} paths originating from each of them must be different edges on the boundary of TT. Therefore, WW contains at least two divide-in-two vertices on the sides of TT and at least one divide-in-two vertex tt on the side of SS. Let the endpoints of WW be ww and w′w^{\prime}. If tt shares a side on the boundary of SS with at least one of ww or w′w^{\prime}, then the monochromatic edges whose endpoints are contained in WW must either exist in an odd number, exist in a pair with different orientations, or exist in a pair that shares an endpoint. In any case, this contradicts Lemma 12. Therefore, it is sufficient to consider the case where tt shares no side on the boundary of SS with ww and w′w^{\prime}. This can occur in {G𝔇​1T}×{G𝔇​3S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}3}\} and {G𝔇​3T,G𝔈​1T}×{G𝔇​13S}\{G^{T}_{\mathfrak{D}3},G^{T}_{\mathfrak{E}1}\}\times\{G^{S}_{\mathfrak{D}13}\}, where the endpoints of WW are on a single side of SS, and tt is located on its opposite side (Figure 32). However, in this case, focusing on the remaining divide-in-two vertices on the side of TT leads to a contradiction for the same reason as in Case C-1-2. ∎

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we demonstrated that a three-piece dissection between a square and an equilateral triangle does not exist. The concept of matching diagrams, which was central to our proof, seems to be broadly applicable as a method for analyzing dissections.

We believe that our approach can be extended to handle the case where pieces can be flipped over. The challenge is to do so without vastly increasing the number of cases that need to be considered. We highlight this and other open problems:

  • •

    Is a three-piece dissection still impossible if flipping is allowed?

  • •

    Is a three-piece dissection still impossible if we allow nonpolygonal (curved) pieces?

  • •

    Are there only a finite number of rectangles that can be dissected into three pieces from a triangle? If so, how can they be enumerated?

  • •

    Are there any other four-piece dissections between an equilateral triangle and a square, aside from Figure 1?

  • •

    Are there any pairs of regular nn-gons and mm-gons that can be dissected into three pieces, where n≠mn\neq m?

During a visit by Tonan Kamata, a discussion with the group—particularly with Motcho Ajisaka and Fueruma (@motcho_tw, @fueruma_suugaku on 𝕏\mathbb{X})—led to the discovery of an oversight in the enumeration of square dissections in the previous version of this paper. We express our deep respect for their open, playful, and curiosity-driven community.
